completeSourceDiscovery.boundaryContinuationRule: a move beginning in lookbehind remains owned by the predecessor chunk

candidateRows: Naturalism has greater intrinsic probability than theism because it is more modest while remaining comparably coherent.
This prior-probability comparison supplies one of Lowder's stated principal grounds for preferring naturalism to theism overall.
After defining modesty and coherence, Lowder argues that theism adds claims beyond supernaturalism and is therefore intrinsically less probable than naturalism.
The required existence of physical reality on naturalism makes physical reality evidence favoring naturalism over theism.
The move directly compares how strongly the competing worldviews predict the existence of the physical reality addressed by the motion.
Lowder says naturalism entails physical reality, whereas a theistic God could create bodies, disembodied minds, or nothing, making physical reality less expected on theism.
The evidence for biological evolution is more probable on naturalism than on theism or special creationism.
This is a complete comparative evidential argument connecting observed biological history to divergent expectations under naturalism and theism.
Lowder surveys biogeography, vestigial organs, natural selection, embryology, and fossils, then argues evolution follows naturally if life exists under naturalism but was unnecessary for God.
The biological role and moral randomness of pain and pleasure are more expected on naturalism than on theism.
The move develops the problem of suffering as comparative evidence by contrasting evolutionary expectations with the moral expectations generated by theism.
Lowder distinguishes useful pain, pain in moral patients, and gratuitous suffering, arguing unguided evolution predicts their distribution while a morally perfect creator could prevent needless pain.
The dependence of human minds on physical brains is evidence favoring naturalism over the existence of an unembodied God.
This argument directly bears on whether physical reality explains mentality or an antecedent divine mind explains physical reality.
Lowder cites stimulation, injury, comparative cognition, and neural development to support mind-brain dependence, contrasting physicalism with theism's unembodied divine mind.
The neurological basis of empathy deficits and moral handicaps is more expected on naturalism than on theism.
The move connects morally consequential brain abnormalities to differing naturalistic and theistic expectations about human moral capacities.
Lowder argues that impaired brain regions can reduce empathy and promote harmful conduct, an outcome expected from indifferent nature but morally surprising if God creates people.
Nonresistant nonbelief is expected on naturalism but conflicts with the availability of relationship expected from a perfectly loving God.
Divine hiddenness supplies a direct comparative test between indifferent nature and the relational intentions attributed to a perfectly loving deity.
Using an absent-father analogy, Lowder describes people open to relationship with God who nevertheless cannot believe, which naturalism permits but perfect divine love makes surprising.
The universe's beginning and fine-tuning point to a spaceless, timeless, immaterial, powerful, personal, and intelligent creator.
The cosmological and fine-tuning inferences directly support the divine creator offered by theism as the explanation of physical reality.
Turek argues that space, matter, and time began, that cosmic constants are precisely set, and that their cause must transcend the universe while possessing power, choice, and intelligence.
Naturalism undermines rational belief because physically determined thoughts would be reactions produced by nonrational causes rather than reasoned conclusions.
The move challenges whether naturalism can consistently support the rational inference and trustworthy cognition required to argue for naturalism itself.
Lowder's earlier claim that naturalism and physicalism provide the better overall explanation of mentality and reality.

Drawing on statements attributed to Crick and Haldane, Turek argues that deterministic molecular accounts make beliefs products of physics and thereby deprive naturalists of grounds for trusting reasoning.
The ordered information in DNA is best explained by an intelligent mind because messages, programs, and codes arise from intelligent sources.
The argument offers specified biological information as affirmative evidence for an intelligent source and therefore for Turek's theistic explanation.
Turek compares DNA's ordered genetic alphabet to meaningful cereal letters, writing in sand, and software, inferring that a code of billions of letters requires a coder.
The regular, goal-directed behavior of nature and living organisms requires an external directing intelligence and supports theism.
This supplies the science component of the cumulative theistic case by treating natural regularity, biological development, and final causality as signs of intelligence.
After completing his treatment of evil, Turek turns to science and develops a sustained teleological argument from orderly laws and directed biological processes.
Turek's cumulative case fails because naturalism can accommodate the cited phenomena while placing them within God merely assumes rather than explains them.
The passage states Lowder's governing rebuttal criterion and applies it across value, induction, causality, time, information, intentionality, and moral obligation.
Turek's claim that naturalism must borrow indispensable concepts from God and cannot explain them.
Lowder answers the CRIMES framework with a counter-framework arguing that incompatibility with naturalism and genuine explanatory success by theism have not been established.
A life-permitting universe does not favor theism because its probability is unknown and its pervasive hostility to life fits naturalism better.
Fine-tuning is a principal component of Turek's creation case, and Lowder offers several independent probabilistic and evidential objections to its theistic use.
Turek's contention that cosmic fine-tuning and a life-permitting universe provide strong evidence for an intelligent creator.
Lowder reframes fine-tuning as life-permission, stresses uncertainty about possible universes, and argues that physical rather than miraculous life favors naturalism.
Current cosmology establishes a beginning of cosmic expansion but not a beginning of the universe, because general relativity fails at the relevant extreme regime.
The argument directly contests the creation premise underlying Turek's cosmological inference and challenges the applicability of its principal scientific support.
Turek's assertion that the universe began from nothing and therefore requires a transcendent immaterial creator.
Lowder distinguishes the Big Bang model from an absolute beginning and argues that singular conditions lie outside general relativity's domain of applicability.
Evolution can produce generally reliable cognition, while neither naturalism nor theism specifically predicts the existence of biological information or life.
It challenges two major components of Turek's cumulative case by supplying a naturalistic route to reliability and denying a comparative theistic prediction of life.
Turek's arguments that naturalistic evolution undermines reason and that biological information requires an intelligent immaterial source.
Lowder argues that truth-sensitive cognitive mechanisms can promote survival and that the bare content of either worldview leaves biological life underpredicted.
Naturalism cannot adequately explain cosmic creation, rational thought, mental causation, or nonphysical realities merely by appealing to physical causes and simplicity.
The passage attacks naturalism's central explanatory thesis and argues that its claimed simplicity omits several indispensable features of reality addressed by theism.
Lowder's initial case that physical causation is sufficient and that naturalism provides the simpler overall explanation of reality.
Turek cites the universe, thought, mind-body effects, logic, mathematics, values, and obligations as realities that a purely molecular account allegedly leaves unexplained.
Scientific explanations of how nature operates do not displace God, because an intelligent creator explains the system whose regular operation science studies.
This directly answers the naturalist appeal to scientific success and defends compatibility between mechanistic explanations and theistic explanation at another level.
Lowder's contention that the historical success of scientific explanation reduces or removes explanatory need for God.
Turek distinguishes explaining a system's operation from explaining its intelligent origin and argues that stable natural laws themselves require divine grounding.
Macroevolution neither explains genetic and structural information nor entails naturalism, since evolutionary processes could themselves operate under divine sustenance.
The move addresses a major naturalistic mechanism, disputes its explanatory adequacy for biological novelty, and denies that accepting it would eliminate God.
Lowder's appeal to macroevolution as a successful naturalistic explanation compatible with his broader worldview.
Turek argues that mutation cannot supply all required biological organization, notes disputes over evolutionary theory, and says God could use evolution regardless.
The amount of pain does not disprove God because treating pain as objectively bad presupposes moral standards, while Christianity supplies restoration and ultimate justice.
Pain and flourishing form a major evidential objection to theism, so the attempt to reverse its moral force and invoke eventual restoration is directly load-bearing.
Lowder's argument that the world's extensive pain and frustrated flourishing are more expected on naturalism than on theism.
Turek recasts the objection from pain as dependent on objective morality and adds the Christian account of a fallen world followed by justice and restoration.
Arguments that minds require brains or that neuroscience proves materialism are question-begging and would undermine trust in scientific reasoning if materialism were true.
The passage directly contests the naturalist account of mentality and adds an epistemic argument that material determination would defeat confidence in neuroscientific conclusions.
Lowder's claim that known minds depend on brains and that neuroscience supports identifying the mind with the physical brain.
Turek invokes a transcendent mind as a proposed exception, accuses naturalism of assuming its conclusion, and argues that determined investigators could not validate materialism.
God may permit temporary honest nonbelief because delayed conversion can produce greater maturity, broader influence, or reduced culpability.
This supplies the theistic explanation needed to resist divine hiddenness as contrary evidence against an interested and responsive God.
Lowder's contention that sincere nonbelievers seek God without receiving adequate confirming evidence.
During Turek's rebuttal, he offers several possible goods that might explain why God delays belief even for a sincere seeker.
Objective moral obligations depend on objective goodness, and objective goodness exists only if God exists.
The move directly defends the moral argument's claimed dependence of binding duties on a divine foundation for objective goodness.
Lowder's argument that genuine moral obligations can exist without God as their ontological foundation.
Turek rejects nontheistic moral obligation by connecting duties to objective goodness and objective goodness exclusively to God's existence.
Humans cannot establish that an evil is gratuitous because only an infinite perspective could trace its consequences through time and eternity.
This is Turek's principal skeptical-theist response to the evidential problem of evil and connects earthly suffering with eventual justice.
Lowder's contention that apparently purposeless or gratuitous evil is evidence weighing against theism.
Turek argues that finite observers cannot follow the ripple effects of suffering, while God can secure goods and justice beyond earthly life.
Evidence favoring theism over one alternative does not establish theism when an insufficiently specified third explanatory hypothesis remains available.
The illustration attacks the comparative-inference structure behind treating observations as decisive for theism without assessing naturalistic alternatives adequately.
Turek's use of selected observations as evidence establishing theism over naturalism beyond reasonable doubt.
Lowder expands his jelly-bean model to a third jar, showing that evidence against one option need not discriminate between the remaining options.
A claim that theism is true beyond reasonable doubt is inadequately supported if major explanatory arguments for atheism and evidential arguments from evil remain substantially unaddressed.
The move challenges the epistemic strength of Turek's overall conclusion by testing whether his case has engaged important competing evidence and objections.
Turek's published and debated claim that the cumulative case establishes theism beyond a reasonable doubt.
Lowder identifies explanatory atheistic arguments, alleged divine contradictions, and evidential evil arguments, then probes whether Turek has addressed them.
If human thought is wholly produced by unguided evolution and physically determined processes, naturalism provides no basis for trusting those thoughts as true.
This is a direct evolutionary and physicalist argument against the reliability of reason, making naturalism allegedly self-undermining as a worldview.
Lowder's naturalistic account of minds, reasoning, and the reliability of conclusions reached by physical brains.
Turek argues that unguided physical causation turns thinkers into determined mechanisms and thereby undermines confidence in naturalistic reasoning itself.
Determinism and the evolutionary origin of cognitive mechanisms do not by themselves reduce those mechanisms' reliability or ability to transmit accurate information.
The response blocks the self-defeat objection by separating a cognitive mechanism's causal origin from its truth-tracking performance and informational function.
Turek's argument that unguided evolution and physical determinism make human reasoning untrustworthy.
Lowder treats the free-will issue as a distraction and argues that created, guided, and unguided perceptual systems can all function reliably.
Naturalism does not entail moral nihilism, because naturalists can consistently endorse objective morality through irreducible moral properties or naturalistic accounts of flourishing.
The distinction directly contests the moral argument's crucial inference from the absence of God to the absence of objective moral truths.
Turek's claim that without God no transcendent moral standard exists and grave abuse cannot be objectively wrong.
Lowder agrees that nihilism has unacceptable implications but denies that naturalism entails nihilism, outlining realist naturalistic positions instead.
Recent experimental support for an RNA-world pathway provides partial confirmation that biological information may have a natural origin, even though the issue remains unsettled.
The response supplies a prospective natural mechanism for biological information and resists treating present uncertainty as decisive evidence for divine design.
Turek's challenge that blind natural forces cannot produce the information-rich sequences found in biological systems.
Lowder appeals to partial confirmation of RNA-world research while distinguishing an open probability judgment from a confident positive origin claim.
Highly specific biological information is positive evidence of intelligence in the same way that an intelligible written message indicates an intelligent source.
The move states the core design inference from complex biological information and distinguishes that inference from merely exploiting a gap in current science.
Lowder's position that biological information may have an unresolved but ultimately natural causal source.
Turek argues that recognizing intelligence from meaningful messages supports making the same evidential inference from billions of informational biological units.
Sparse transitional fossils do not undermine evolution because fossilization, preservation, and discovery are incomplete, while even one transitional fossil counts against special creation.
This directly defends evolutionary evidence used in Lowder's naturalistic case against an audience challenge based on gaps in the fossil record.
The audience claim that fossil scarcity and Gould's remarks support a worldwide flood or special creation rather than evolution.
An audience member invokes fossil gaps and Gould as evidence against evolution; Lowder distinguishes evolutionary predictions from assumptions about fossilization and preservation.
Design analogies do not clearly favor a disembodied designer when their full evidence concerns embodied minds, though mental existence and moral agency provide some genuine evidence for theism.
The move both challenges a major design inference and carefully identifies evidence that Lowder concedes favors theism, clarifying his comparative method.
The audience analogy that a constructed room requires workers and therefore the much larger universe must require an intelligent creator.
Lowder answers a room-building analogy by warning against selective analogical reasoning, then distinguishes weak fine-tuning claims from stronger evidence involving minds and moral agents.

Moral disagreement does not refute objective morality, but extensive historical moral confusion is evidence favoring naturalism because a perfect God would be expected to communicate fundamental duties clearly.
This preserves moral realism under naturalism while turning historical moral disagreement into comparative evidence against theism's predicted divine guidance.
Turek's claim that changing moral beliefs are compatible with an objective moral standard grounded beyond human societies.
After Turek argues that moral progress presupposes an external standard, Lowder agrees about objectivity but argues that pervasive confusion is unexpected under perfect divine guidance.
Contingent reality requires God as a continuously sustaining, noncontingent and fully actual cause, so creation would cease to exist without divine conservation.
The argument presents divine sustenance, not merely an initial creative act, as a fundamental explanatory dependence of the entire contingent universe.
In response to a neutral question about divine withdrawal, Turek compares God sustaining the universe to a band sustaining music and grounds this in contingency.
Even granting divine sustenance as evidence for theism, the universe's continued existence counterbalances it because only theism posits an external agent capable of ending physical reality.
This is a direct comparative-probability rebuttal that attempts to reverse or neutralize a central theistic explanation of the universe's ongoing existence.
Turek's assertion that the contingent universe requires God to create and continuously sustain it in existence.
Lowder first notes that sustaining-cause claims are often asserted without argument, then conditionally grants the claim and offers continued existence as countervailing evidence.
Science depends on prior philosophical commitments, and excluding intelligent causes before examining evidence is a philosophical restriction rather than a scientific conclusion.
The move supports theism's compatibility with scientific inquiry while challenging methodological exclusions that would prevent intelligent explanation from being considered.
Asked about science and faith, Turek lists metaphysical presuppositions of inquiry, stresses that evidence requires interpretation, and criticizes prior exclusion of intelligent causes.
Naturalism prioritizes physical over mental causal reality without entailing scientism or materialism, and it can consistently affirm autonomous abstract or acausal realities.
This defines the precise naturalist position at issue and blocks a central theistic critique that treats naturalism as denying every nonphysical or nonscientific reality.
Turek's account of philosophy as indispensable to science and the broader suggestion that atheistic naturalism excludes necessary metaphysical realities.
Lowder rejects scientism as self-undermining, maps causal naturalism against supernaturalism, and explains that naturalism need not deny abstract objects or other acausal realities.

Theism does not uniquely ground science's presuppositions because naturalism can accommodate logic, mathematics, reliable perception, uniformity, reason, and orderly laws, sometimes with better predictive fit.
The extended closing reply addresses a principal theistic case about the foundations of science and offers naturalistic explanations or compatibility claims across its major components.
Turek's contention that morality, free will, logic, realism, uniformity, reason, natural laws, and causality presuppose God and underwrite science.
Lowder reviews the proposed presuppositions of science, disputes that positing God explains them, and argues that evolutionary naturalism handles cognition and perceptual reliability.
Moral laws need no lawgiver merely by being laws, since morality can be understood alongside discovered and noncreated laws of nature, logic, mathematics, and rationality.
This directly attacks the inference from objective moral law to God, one of the debate's principal arguments for theism as morality's foundation.
Turek's argument that every law requires a lawgiver and that the existence of moral law therefore establishes a divine moral lawgiver.
Lowder distinguishes laws that are given from laws that are discovered and argues that necessary, nonoriginating laws do not require a personal legislator.

Lowder's comparative case remains unanswered because naturalism's greater intrinsic probability and supporting evidence concerning physical reality and moral handicaps have not been substantively disputed.
This is the final synthesis of Lowder's case, identifying the governing explanatory criterion and claiming that his major naturalistic advantages survived the debate unrebutted.
Turek's overall theistic case and its failure, according to Lowder, to answer naturalism's prior-probability and comparative-evidence arguments.
At the end of his closing statement, Lowder returns to explanatory balance, intrinsic probability, physical reality, and moral handicaps as allegedly unanswered considerations.
Theism better explains creation, reason, information, morality, evil, and science than naturalism does.
This explicitly states Turek's overall comparative conclusion and identifies the six principal explanatory domains supporting the theistic side.
Following Lowder's closing recap and applause, Turek begins his own summary by restating the principal domains in which he claims theism has superior explanatory power.
Objective moral comparisons require a standard beyond human individuals, which naturalism has not coherently supplied.
The argument supplies Turek's central moral case for a transcendent standard and directly challenges naturalism's capacity to ground objective morality.
Lowder's claim that morality can be objective or adequately explained without God.
Turek compares judging persons with comparing maps against an external place, arguing that moral judgments likewise presuppose an objective reference beyond those being judged.
Ethical disagreement is better explained by theistic free will than by deterministic natural laws governing brains.
This directly contests an evidential argument for naturalism and connects moral disagreement to Turek's broader case for agency and freedom under theism.
Lowder's contention that ethical disagreement provides evidence favoring naturalism over theism.
Turek argues that uniform physical determination should produce agreement, whereas actual disagreement indicates freely chosen ethical judgments not wholly controlled by natural laws.
Much moral disagreement results from willfully suppressing known moral duties rather than from the absence of objective morality.
This offers a distinct explanatory mechanism for moral disagreement, supporting the larger claim that disagreement does not undermine objective moral truth.
Lowder's use of widespread ethical disagreement as evidence against the theistic account of morality.
Turek attributes many disputes to motivated denial: people recognize a moral constraint but suppress it when it obstructs what they want to do.
Lowder's naturalistic case depends upon conceptual resources that are available only within a theistic worldview.
This introduces the organizing charge for the remainder of Turek's closing argument: naturalism allegedly presupposes what only theism can explain.
Lowder's cumulative naturalistic case and its appeal to probability, reason, morality, and scientific order.
After finishing the disagreement discussion, Turek transitions to a general internal critique alleging that Lowder must borrow theistic foundations to formulate naturalistic arguments.
Naturalistic probability arguments rely on purposive mathematical and logical laws that are grounded in a transcendent mind.
The move challenges Lowder's core probability framework by claiming its logical and mathematical preconditions receive an explanation only from theism.
Lowder's probability-based case for naturalism and his argument that abstract laws do not require a lawgiver.
Turek contrasts naturalism's denial of cosmic purpose with Lowder's reliance on mathematics, logic, and probability, then grounds those regularities in God's nature.
If blind physical laws completely determine thought, human reasoning cannot justify believing naturalism or any other proposition true.
This is Turek's principal self-defeat argument against naturalistic accounts of reason and directly concerns whether naturalism can support rational belief.
Lowder's claim that naturalism can account for generally reliable cognition and rational inference.
Turek argues that wholly determined molecular processes eliminate genuine rational agency, thereby undercutting confidence in the truth of naturalism itself.
Naturalistic moral complaints about God presuppose the objective moral standard that naturalism itself cannot explain.
This internal critique connects Lowder's arguments from morally objectionable features of reality to Turek's claim that objective morality requires theism.
Lowder's moral objections concerning how God would govern or permit features of the actual universe.
Turek contends that objections to divine governance require an objective measure of wrongness, while maintaining that Lowder has not grounded such a measure naturalistically.
Creation, reason, information, morality, evil, and science require a prior intelligent personal agent rather than naturalism.
This is the closing synthesis of Turek's entire comparative case, explicitly linking every major explanatory domain to a personal intelligent cause.
Turek condenses his case into a general inference from several immaterial aspects of reality to an antecedent intelligent personal agent.
Naturalism requires unsupported commitments across creation, reason, information, morality, evil, and the success of science.
The passage delivers Turek's final cumulative comparison by summarizing the alleged explanatory liabilities of naturalism in all six major domains.
Lowder's overall contention that naturalism has the better balance of prior probability and explanatory accuracy.
Turek closes by listing what he regards as naturalism's unexplained or implausible consequences for cosmic origins, rationality, biological information, moral facts, evil, and science.
